title: Selected Passages from the Two Epistles
subtitle: From the First and Second Epistles General of Peter
source: Text drawn from the King James Version (1611, public domain). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: A living hope
sections.framing: The first epistle opens with a doxology unlike any other in the New Testament. Peter is writing, probably from Rome, to scattered communities of Christians in the provinces of Asia Minor who are beginning to suffer for the Name. Before he speaks of their trials he tells them what they have been given. The hope, he says, is not a wish but a thing alive, born from the Resurrection of Christ, kept in heaven for them as gold is kept in a treasury, and revealing itself even now in a love that does not need to see in order to believe.
paragraphs: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations:
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
notes: The verb in 'hath begotten us again' is the same Peter heard on the lips of Christ in the conversation with Nicodemus: a man must be born again. Peter writes as one who knows what the second birth has cost and given him.
First Peter is generally dated to the early sixties, written from 'Babylon' (5:13), a name the early Church used for Rome.

sections.title: A chosen generation
sections.framing: Having reminded the scattered Christians of what they have been given, Peter turns to who they have been made. He gathers up the great titles God once gave to Israel at Sinai and applies them, unhesitatingly, to a handful of believers in Pontus and Bithynia. The Church, he says, is no afterthought: it is the people God has been gathering all along. Their calling, like Israel's, is to be a kingdom of priests, that is, to stand between the world and God and offer the world up to Him.
paragraphs: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light;
Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.
notes: Peter is quoting Exodus 19:5-6, the words spoken to Moses at Sinai. The shift of address is the whole theology of the New Testament in two verses.
'A peculiar people' renders a Greek term meaning 'a people for God's own possession.' The English word once carried that sense; it now misleads, and modern translations read 'a people of his own.'

sections.title: The shepherd of the flock
sections.framing: Near the end of the first epistle Peter speaks to the presbyters, the elders, of the churches. He speaks as one of them. He does not invoke his place among the Twelve or his commission by the lake; he calls himself 'a witness of the sufferings of Christ' and a fellow elder. To his brothers in the pastoral office he gives the counsel he himself received: feed the flock, and do not domineer over it. The chief Shepherd, when He appears, will weigh how the under-shepherds have kept His sheep.
paragraphs: The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed:
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
notes: Peter never forgot the threefold 'Feed my sheep' the risen Christ had laid on him by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21). The verb here is the same.
The image of the 'chief Shepherd' is the Old Testament hope (Ezekiel 34) brought into the new dispensation. The under-shepherds will give account to Him.

sections.title: Cast all your care
sections.framing: The first epistle closes with a counsel that the Orthodox Church reads at compline and that pilgrims write on the walls of cells. Peter, who once sank in the waves for looking at them instead of at Christ, now tells the persecuted to set down the weight they were not meant to carry. He does not say their cares are small. He says God minds about them, and that the proud man's resistance and the anxious man's clutching are at root one sickness, the refusal to let God be God.
paragraphs: Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
notes: 'God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble' is a quotation of Proverbs 3:34 (Septuagint), the same verse James 4:6 cites. Peter and James, the two pillars of the Jerusalem church, are evidently drawing from a common catechesis.
'He careth for you' uses a Greek verb (melei) implying personal concern, not abstract oversight. The Fathers note its tenderness.

sections.title: Grow in grace
sections.framing: The second epistle, written near the end of Peter's life and aware of it, is a charge laid on the next generation. He warns of false teachers, recalls the holy mountain where he saw the glory, and ends with a sentence that has been read as his own last word to the Church. The Christian life, he says, is not a height to be reached and held. It is a growth, and the soil it grows in is the knowledge of Christ, who is Himself the ground and the goal.
paragraphs: Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.
But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
notes: Second Peter is the apostle's testament; he says explicitly that he writes knowing his departure is at hand (1:14-15). Tradition places it in Rome shortly before his crucifixion under Nero, around 67.
The doxology at the end is one of only two in the New Testament addressed directly to Christ (the other is 2 Timothy 4:18), an early witness to apostolic worship of the Son as God.
